content: Butterfly weed, scientifically known as Asclepias tuberosa, is also referred to by various other names, including Canada root, Chigger flower, Fluxroot, Indian paintbrush, Indian posy, Orange milkweed, Orange Swallow-wort, Pleurisy root, Silky Swallow-wort, Tuber root, Yellow milkweed, White-root, and Windroot. This plant is a species of milkweed native to eastern North America. It typically grows to a height of 1 to 2 feet (approximately 30 to 60 cm) and produces clusters of vibrant orange or yellow flowers that bloom from early summer through early fall. The leaves of the butterfly weed are arranged in a spiral pattern, are lanceolate in shape, and measure between 5 to 12 cm in length and 2 to 3 cm in width. This plant thrives in dry, sandy, or gravelly soils but has also been observed growing along stream margins. Its common name, butterfly weed, is derived from its ability to attract butterflies, which are drawn to the plant's bright coloration and abundant nectar production. Additionally, it serves as a larval food source for the Queen butterfly. In terms of identification, butterfly weed bears a resemblance to the Lanceolate milkweed (Asclepias lanceolata). However, it can be distinguished by its larger number of flowers and its hairy stems, which notably do not exude a milky sap when broken. This plant is most commonly found in fields with dry soil conditions. Butterfly weed is also known by other common names, such as Canada-root, Chigger flower, Indian posy, Orange-root, Orange Swallow-wort, Tuber root, White-root, Windroot, and Yellow or Orange milkweed. There are three recognized subspecies of Asclepias tuberosa: 1. Asclepias tuberosa interior, which is native to the central United States. 2. Asclepias tuberosa rolfsii (commonly referred to as Rolf's Milkweed), found in the southeastern United States. 3. Asclepias tuberosa tuberosa, which is native to the eastern United States.
